title: Spacecraft and Payload Data Handling
short_title: Mars Express spacecraft and payload data handling
organisation: European Space Agency (ESA Publications; authors from ESA/ESTEC, ESA/ESOC, ESA/ESAC and instrument institutes)
status_notes: Published book chapter in ESA SP-1291 'Mars Express: The Scientific Investigations', June 2009 (PDF p. 1), part 'Operations and Archiving' (PDF p. 2), printed pages 257-276.
summary:
A chapter of ESA SP-1291, 'Mars Express: The Scientific Investigations' (June 2009), by J. Zender (ESTEC), F. Delhaise (ESOC), C. Arviset (ESAC) and some thirty co-authors from ESA and the instrument teams. It traces Mars Express data from the spacecraft through the ground segment and the instrument teams to the Planetary Science Archive (PSA).

The ground-segment sections are the most relevant to this wiki. They define the processing levels (level 0 raw telemetry, level 1 cleaned, merged and time-ordered packets, level 1a separated by instrument, up to level 3) and their CODMAC and PDS equivalents. They describe the ESOC Operations Control Centre shared by Rosetta, Mars Express and Venus Express: the SCOS-2000-based Mission Control System (real-time housekeeping processing, command verification, out-of-limit checks, calibration, UTC time stamping with an accuracy below 2 ms, command history), the Data Distribution System (DDS) built on the Generic Data Disposition System (GDDS), the Mission Planning System and the Flight Operations Procedure system. They explain how NCTRS receives Earth-reception-time-stamped telemetry from the ground stations and forwards telecommands, and how the DDS handles XML requests (standing orders, web or FTP), retrieves data from the SCOS-2000 packet and file archives over CORBA, and delivers by web, FTP or CD-ROM, with SFDU-based formats and a ten-year archive of level 1 data.

The later sections cover the PDS standard (ODL keyword=value labels, data dictionary, catalogue files, EAICDs), the archive process and peer review, the PSA user interfaces, and the datasets of each instrument (ASPERA-3, HRSC, MaRS, OMEGA, PFS, SPICAM, MARSIS) and SPICE kernels.

contents.title: Dissemination of Mission Raw Data via the Mars Express DDS
Scientific Processing and Data Archive Preparation
ASPERA-3 (Analyser of Space Plasmas and Energetic Neutral Atoms)
OMEGA (Observatoire pour la Minéralogie, l'Eau, les Glaces et l'Activité)
SPICAM (Spectroscopy for Investigation of Characteristics of the Atmosphere of Mars)
MARSIS (Mars Advanced Radar for Subsurface and Ionosphere Sounding)

key_points.text: Processing levels in the Mars Express archive plan: level 0 raw telemetry as received at the ground station; level 1 cleaned, merged, time-ordered data in packet format; level 1a separated by instrument; level 1b sorted by data type and mode; level 2 calibrated; level 3 higher-level products.
Rosetta, Mars Express and Venus Express share nearly identical data management systems at the ESOC Operations Control Centre, to reduce cost, risk and development time.

The SCOS-2000-based MCS processes housekeeping data in real time (command verification, out-of-limit detection, calibration) and time-stamps telemetry by converting on-board time to UTC with an accuracy below 2 ms.

The DDS is based on the Generic Data Disposition System (GDDS) and also produces raw data media for permanent archiving; the MCS itself has no remote access, so external users reach mission data only via the DDS.

NCTRS is the ground-station interface of the MCS: it receives telemetry already time-stamped with Earth Reception Time, forwards telecommands to the stations, and stores tracking data (antenna angles, range, Doppler).

Mission products include payload science data, all platform and payload housekeeping and auxiliary data (TC history, station visibility, orbit, attitude); a common SFDU-based interchange standard is used, and all level 1 data are archived for ten years after the end of the mission.

The SCOS-2000 mission archive has a packet archive (historical TM, TC and derived data) and a file archive (flight dynamics and planning data); GDDS requests come as standing orders, via the web interface or as FTP request files, expressed in a recursive XML query language.

The DDS server initiates archive retrievals on the MCS via a CORBA-based interface and delivers data online, by FTP or on CD-ROM; online retrieval embeds the data as a byte stream in the XML response and is meant only for previews.

The PDS standard was chosen early for Rosetta, Mars Express and SMART-1; it uses the Object Description Language (keyword = value labels) with keywords defined in the Planetary Science Data Dictionary.

Section headings in the side margin are interleaved with body text in the extraction (e.g. '2.1 Overview  2. The Ground Segment'). The section 4 heading prints only 'Planetary Science' in the text layer (the margin heading is truncated); 'Planetary Science Archive' is inferred from the content. The lead author's e-mail address on PDF p. 3 is omitted. The DDID reference (RO-ESC-IF-5003) corresponds to the library items ro-esc-if-5003-ddid-c2 and mex-esc-if-5003-b5.
